base_instructions.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would. Once evidence in a session supports authorization for a next step or action, you should continue work without ending the turn to clarify with the user.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless given explicit instructions to do so, or instructed to do so as part of an explicitly-invoked skill or plugin. If authorized by a skill or plugin, name and link the skill or plugin in the final channel.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason. Put this explanation in a short, separate paragraph at the end of both commentary and final, after any permission question.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

When the user's prompt indicates a request for action, such as "can you...", "I want to...", "help me..." and similar expressions, treat these as instructions to do the work and take action. Do not stop at acknowledging capability (e.g. "Yes…"), proposing a plan, or offering to continue. Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment. 

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a lucid communicator. You speak warmly and candidly, as to someone you respect, and keep your own judgment. You disagree when you have reason; reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

Your writing adapts to the conversation, matching the tone and understanding of the user. Make sure to state the main point clearly and early, then develop it with the explanation and detail the reader needs. Let each sentence build on what came before. Develop the points that matter and provide enough support to be useful. 

Use plain, simple language: familiar words, concrete examples, and precise verbs. Prefer active voice and direct statements. Write in connected prose. Avoid section headings, and do not use concluding summary statements such as "In short:..", "The simplest mental model is:...".

Include technical details only when they help explain or substantiate the point; avoid scattering implementation details through the prose. Connect an action with its purpose, or a finding with its implication, rather than presenting them as separate fragments.

Default to using clear, concise paragraphs, each developing one main idea. Use lists only when the information is genuinely parallel, sequential, or easier to compare, and avoid nested lists unless the hierarchy cannot be expressed clearly in prose. 

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer." or "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely" or hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives. 

State the intended action directly. Avoid adding what you won't do or what something is not, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

Avoid unnecessary apologies and self-blame. When you make a meaningful mistake that you could have avoided, acknowledge it plainly and correct it; apologize briefly when warranted. Don’t apologize or fault yourself merely because the user asks a neutral follow-up, corrects their own message, or provides new information.

## Technical communication

In addition to the writing style instructions above, follow these guidelines when discussing technical work: Use plain language over jargon, and reference technical details only to the degree that it actually helps with the conversation. Communicate complex concepts in a clear and cohesive manner. Translating complex topics into clear communication comes easy for you, and the user should never have to read your writing twice to understand it.

Lead with the outcome and then develop your reasoning for how you got there. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits. 

Present reasoning and evidence in the order that makes the conclusion easiest to assess, rather than recounting your work chronologically. Summarize routine verification instead of listing every check. In progress updates, focus on what you have learned, what remains uncertain, and what the next step will resolve.

### Writing PR descriptions

Lead the description with the concrete problem and resulting behavior. Use a concrete trigger and before/after example when helpful. Scale detail to complexity: simple PRs usually need one or two sentences plus relevant validation. Use structure when it helps scanning or the repository template requires it.

Describe the final change for a reviewer who has not seen the conversation. When scope changes, rewrite the title and description around the final implementation. Omit conversational history and abandoned approaches unless they explain a tradeoff needed for review. Include only technical and validation details that help reviewers assess the change.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

When available, you can use the `functions.request_user_input_async` tool to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. You can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Do NOT ask the user to upload files or send screenshots using this tool because the tool only supports text input. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 60 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermediate commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information. 

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization. 

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead. 

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding. 

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- Batch independent searches and reads in one functions.exec using await Promise.allSettled([...]); inspect every result. Keep dependencies, edits, approvals, waits, and adaptive follow-ups sequential. Avoid unnecessary output.
- When calling `functions.exec`, parallelize independent tool calls by awaiting Promises. Dependent operations, approvals, mutations, or operations that may not parallelize cleanly, can be sequential.
- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.
- Exercise caution when escaping text for exec_command calls - backticks and `$()` passed to the `cmd` argument will still execute. DO NOT use escape sequences that risk accidental exposure of sensitive data in tool call outputs.
- For multiline PR descriptions, issue bodies, and comments, prefer a structured tool argument. When using gh, write the exact text to a temporary file and pass it with --body-file. Preserve actual newlines and intentional literal escapes.
- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.
- Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.
- Keep implementation details out of product (e.g. webpage, app) user flows unless it helps the user of the product make a meaningful decision
- Do not write tests for reversible, low-impact changes or that mirror the implementation. If you do choose to verify your work with tests, make sure that the tests are meaningful and necessary to verify implementation.
- Run tests appropriate to the change and complete required checks. Once those pass, broaden or repeat testing only when new changes, failures, or unresolved concerns justify it; otherwise, continue toward completing the task.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill. If explicit user instructions conflict with a skill's instructions, prioritize the user's instructions. 

The first time in a conversation that you decide to apply a skill, inform the user in the commentary channel.

If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause, or leave requested work unfinished, name and link to the exact SKILL.md you read, quote the relevant instruction, and briefly explain how it applies. Distinguish explicit skill requirements from your interpretation. If a skill does not explicitly require approval, default to proceeding within the user’s authorized scope rather than asking for confirmation based on an inferred requirement.

## When to use a skill

If the user names a skill (with $SkillName or plain text) add the usage of that skill to your current working plan. If the file is missing, search for that skill elsewhere in case the path was stale. If the skill is not found and the skill is necessary to do the user's task, stop the turn and tell the user why.

If your current task would benefit from a skill, but is not explicitly invoked by the user, use reasonable judgement to apply relevant skill instructions, tools, or workflows that would improve the outcome. Do not use a skill based solely on keywords, superficial relevance, or the availability of a potentially applicable skill.

## How to use skills

Open and read the skill according to its location: filesystem skills should be read from the filesystem, environment-owned skills should be access via the corresponding environment, and orchestrator skills should be discovered by calling `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"orchestrator"}}`, selecting the matching package, and passing its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. Avoid re-reading skills when possible. 

When a `SKILL.md` file references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism as the skill. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`. For orchestrator skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

# Apps (Connectors)

Apps (Connectors) can be explicitly triggered in user messages in the format `[$app-name](app://{{connector_id}})`. Apps can also be implicitly triggered as long as the context suggests usage of available apps.
An app is equivalent to a set of MCP tools within the `codex_apps` MCP.
An installed app's MCP tools are either provided to you already, or can be lazy-loaded through the `tool_search` tool. If `tool_search` is available, the apps that are searchable by `tools_search` will be listed by it.
Do not additionally call list_mcp_resources or list_mcp_resource_templates for apps.

# Plugins

A plugin is a local bundle of skills, MCP servers, and apps.

## How to use plugins

- Skill naming: If a plugin contributes skills, those skill entries are prefixed with plugin_name: in the Skills list.
- MCP naming: Plugin-provided MCP tools keep standard MCP identifiers such as mcp__server__tool; use tool provenance to tell which plugin they come from.
- Trigger rules: If the user explicitly names a plugin, prefer capabilities associated with that plugin for that turn.
- Relationship to capabilities: Plugins are not invoked directly. Use their underlying skills, MCP tools, and app tools to help solve the task.
- Relevance: Determine what a plugin can help with from explicit user mention or from the plugin-associated skills, MCP tools, and apps exposed elsewhere in this turn.
- Missing/blocked: If the user requests a plugin that does not have relevant callable capabilities for the task, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. # Write run judge brief

You judge one run of a writing Skill. The Skill takes a brief with source material, writes one first draft, has a fresh checker compare the draft with the material (at most twice), validates each report, repairs supported defects, and either delivers the draft or stops without delivering.

You are given a run directory. Read `work/source.md` (the brief and all supplied material), `response.md` (what the user received), `delivered.md` (the delivered draft, where the run delivered one), and every file under `evidence/` (drafts, checker reports and the writer's dispositions, where the run kept them). Read only these staged files and criteria.md. Read nothing else. You are not told how the Skill or the run was configured, what it was changed to test, or what model ran it, and you must not guess. A checker's or the writer's own approval is an argument to weigh, never evidence. Judge from the source yourself.

Where the run delivered nothing, judge the last draft in the evidence and mark it as not delivered.

## Criteria

| F1 | Does every assertion, quotation, attribution and implication stay within the supplied material, including uncertainty, chronology, causal limits and author perspective? Cite any unsupported addition or dropped caveat. Count-size judgements need a supplied comparison. |
| G2 | Do the required parts perform distinct useful jobs? The text carries a headline, a standfirst, a byline, a lead, one or more sections and an ending, in that order, each doing its own job. For a customer account: the customer's situation, action, results and appraisal, a truthful publisher stance, the customer left an acting party, and a call to action built from supplied offers, links or contact routes. |
| L1 | Does the prose sound professionally written in the resolved language, with native idiom and syntax, without importing one language's phrasing into the other? Separate this from locale mechanics — spelling, punctuation, number and date forms are not L1. |

## What to write

Write one Markdown file at the path you are given, in the run directory:

1. **Outcome**: delivered or stopped; how many comparisons ran; whether the delivered prose is identical to the last prose a checker saw.
2. **F1**, on the judged draft: pass or fail, citing every unsupported addition, changed term, changed subject, scope, date, modality or certainty, dropped caveat, invented event or personal attribute. Check translated terms in both directions: could something fall under the draft's term and not the source's, or the reverse, in this context? Keep unknown apart from absent.
3. **G1, G2, P1, W1, L1, L2** on the same draft: pass, fail or skipped individually, with passages and reader effect, using criteria.md. Separate a professional-idiom judgement from locale mechanics. The invoking user is Thomas Barregren; an explicitly disclosed invocation-derived byline naming him is allowed.
4. **Bridges into quotations.** A *bridge* is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. Take every quotation in the judged draft, in the order it appears, and give one line each:

   - the bridge, quoted in full, and the quotation it introduces, quoted in full;
   - **its class**, exactly one of:
     - **(a)** it states what the quotation then says, adding no understanding of its own — a reader who has read the bridge meets the quotation as the bridge said again;
     - **(b)** it names the subject, the occasion or the attribution and no more;
     - **(c)** it carries a fact the quotation does not carry.

     Choose one class and give the words in the bridge that put it there. Where a bridge could be read two ways, say so and give both readings with the reason you chose. Naming the subject a quotation goes on to speak about is not by itself class (a): class (a) is the bridge having already delivered what the quotation is there to deliver, so that the quotation adds nothing the reader did not already have.
   - whether a quotation stands with no bridge at all, which is its own answer and not a class.

   Then answer three things in one sentence each: how many bridges of each class the draft carries; whether the draft attributes to an interviewer, or otherwise puts in an interviewer's mouth, any question or utterance the supplied material does not itself carry, quoting it if so; and whether any bridge asserts something the supplied material does not support, quoting it if so.
5. **Quoted speech**: whether the meaning, stance, degree of certainty, any reservation, and the speaker's own voice in each quotation are what the source carries or have moved; and whether any quotation the material offers and permits is missing from the draft altogether.
6. **Intermediate**: for every checker finding in the evidence, and for every finding the reply mentions where no report file exists, one line: the passage, the allegation, what the writer did, and your class — supported repair, disputed caution, wrong finding accepted, right finding rejected, wrong finding rejected (correct), or not judgeable from the evidence. Then say whether a real defect you found under F1 or under point 4 was seen by no checker.
7. **Stop or delivery**: a valid stop, a false stop, a valid delivery, or a delivery that should not have happened, with the reason.

Give a complete judgement with all requested sections. Save it as judgement.md and include it in your final response. Do not inspect traces or model identities. Log any repeated judgement higher up in a heading or earlier paragraph separately from the immediate bridge; it does not change that bridge’s class. For mixed bridges, record any substantive pre-echo clause as well as the independent fact, rather than hiding the clause under class (c).

Delivered below as a British English case study (`en_GB`), with frontmatter and no technique; the case-study genre specifies none. The byline uses Thomas Barregren because the brief names no author.

```markdown
---
kntnt:
  genre: casestudy
  technique: none
  language: en_GB
---

# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’
```

Two source comparisons completed; the final comparison left no unresolved findings. No call to action was supplied, so the ending carries Vale’s appraisal. The trial summary provides no measures of repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

Skill scratch was removed after both checkers finished. The requested observer captures remain.

# Source and quotation comparison

Invocation: `/write --genre=casestudy --language=en_GB --output=response source.md`.
Material compared: the complete `source.md` and the complete supplied `draft.md`, including title, standfirst, headings, byline and quotations. Source and target language are English. This review concerns source support and quotation fidelity only.

## Findings

### F1 — The title presents retention as accomplished

**Draft:** “Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs”

**Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source establishes the manager’s approval of continued use. The headline’s ordinary factual reading says Fenwick continues to retain/use the schedule for new jobs. Approval and implementation are different states. The source does not establish implementation after approval.

**Concrete test:** The manager could approve continued use, with that approval awaiting an account renewal or another implementation step; no subsequent new job need have used the schedule. This fits the supplied account and makes the approval true without establishing the headline’s accomplished continuation. Conversely, staff could continue using a schedule without managerial approval; the supplied statement “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” excludes that as an account of this case. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick’s manager approves continued use of its shared schedule for new jobs”. This preserves the headline’s subject matter and warranted certainty, while identifying the established decision.

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

### F2 — The standfirst adds a sequence not established by the material

**Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Also: “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Also: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source states when the trial began, its duration, the summary’s date and the postponement’s condition. It does not say that the manager postponed adding the backlog after the six weeks had elapsed. “After” adds a chronological relationship and implies a completed trial before the postponement.

**Concrete test:** A six-week trial beginning on 20 January could run until 3 March. Its 23 February summary could be an interim summary, and the manager could postpone adding the backlog on 23 February while approving continued use for new jobs. All supplied statements can hold, while “postponed … after a six-week … trial” fails. Neither “trial summary” nor its date explicitly rules out an interim summary. Conversely, postponement after some six-week trial does not establish that this trial began in January or that a team review was its condition; the source expressly supplies those facts. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** Replace the standfirst’s first sentence with: “Fenwick Instrument Repairs’ manager approved continued use of its Benchline schedule for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog pending the team’s review of its status definitions.”

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

Both quotations reproduce the supplied email extract word for word. The first comprises the two consecutive sentences of Vale’s first answer; the second comprises the two consecutive sentences of Vale’s second answer. No remarks have been welded together, paraphrased into quotation marks or translated. The shift from double quotation marks in the source to single quotation marks in the draft is punctuation around the same quoted content, not a substantive alteration.

The draft correctly identifies an email interview and introduces the second quotation with “wrote”. It does not portray the extract as speech, a workshop visit, facial expression or emotional reaction. The source expressly states: “Publication of the extract was approved by Vale.” The draft invents no approval process or approval status.

Source-support quotation findings: none. Translation findings: none; no translation took place.

# Source and quotation comparison: draft 2

## Scope and result

Read the complete `source.md` and complete `draft-2.md`, including the title, standfirst, byline, headings and both quotations. The supplied source is the complete package. This comparison covers factual support, attribution, strength, scope, chronology, implications and quotation fidelity. It does not assess general editorial or mechanical choices.

**Result: no source-support findings and no translation findings.** The byline is authorised by the invocation identifying Thomas Barregren; it is not treated as an unsupported attribution because the source brief supplies no author.

The accounting below quotes the source in its original English. References to “the workshop”, “the team” and “the manager” are resolved within the source: Fenwick Instrument Repairs, its workshop team and Priya Vale. The draft does not attribute facts to unnamed outside authorities.

## Complete claim accounting

### Title and standfirst

1. **Draft:** “Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs”.

   **Source:** “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” And: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

   **Comparison:** The manager, product and new-job scope are supported. In the context of a case-study headline, “approves” reports the documented approval; it does not supply a new approval date or an approval for every workshop. “Benchline” names the schedule selected and configured in the source. “Continued” is elaborated in the body, which also preserves the backlog exclusion. No change to the subject, certainty or whose decision this was.

   **Difference test:** Approval covering the backlog would differ from the source, but the title restricts the approval to new jobs, and the standfirst expressly states the postponement. A general recommendation for other workshops would differ, but the title names Fenwick’s manager and Fenwick’s use, with no general recommendation. Neither reading establishes a defect in the passage as written.

2. **Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions.”

   **Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Also: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”

   **Comparison:** The organisational attribution to Fenwick reports its manager’s workshop decision. “Pending a review” preserves the dependency expressed by “until the team had reviewed”; it does not say the review has happened. “Job status definitions” refers to the statuses for jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work. Neither passage specifies the backlog’s size or the date when it would be added.

   **Difference test:** A completed review or an already-added backlog would fail the source’s postponement and pending condition; the draft asserts neither. An unrelated review would not satisfy “a review of job status definitions”. No supported reading changes the decision or condition.

3. **Draft:** “For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.”

   **Source:** Brief: “Write a journalistic customer case in British English for independent repair workshop managers.” And: “Show what the customer changed, what the trial established and what its manager would approach differently.” Material: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” And: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” And: “The summary and interview establish the team’s reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

   **Comparison:** This is the author’s supported framing of the case for the brief’s audience. It refers to the reported setup process and the summary’s evidential reach. It adds no technical effect or measured outcome. The body supplies both the visibility report and the unmeasured outcomes, preserving the limits.

   **Difference test:** Measured faster repairs or a universal recommendation would exceed the material, but neither is asserted by “how the team set up job statuses” or “what its trial summary could establish”. “Could establish” does not convert the reported experience into a measured improvement. No finding.

### Byline and opening paragraph

4. **Draft:** “By Thomas Barregren”.

   **Support:** The invocation identifies the user as Thomas Barregren, and the brief says: “No author name or call to action is supplied.”

   **Comparison:** Byline treatment is expressly resolved in the assignment. No finding.

5. **Draft:** “In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.”

   **Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” The preceding sentence names Fenwick Instrument Repairs.

   **Comparison:** Same organisation, team, start month, duration, trial and shared bench schedule. The six-week modifier applies to the trial, not to training or rollout. No inference of a particular January start day or February end day.

   **Difference test:** A six-week deployment beginning outside January, or six weeks of training, would differ, but neither meets the draft or source statement. No difference in the claims.

6. **Draft:** “The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments”.

   **Source:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.”

   **Comparison:** Same workshop and instrument categories. “The workshop” substitutes an established referent. Neither statement excludes additional instrument categories or says that every repair is of one of these types.

   **Difference test:** Brass-only services would fail both statements; additional services would be compatible with both. No difference.

7. **Draft:** “jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets.”

   **Source:** “Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets.”

   **Comparison:** Same job categories, separation, paper medium and chronology before the trial. The past-perfect tense situates the previous arrangement relative to the trial without adding an earlier date or duration. It does not assert that paper disappeared entirely.

   **Difference test:** One combined sheet would fail both; continued paper use for some other purpose could coexist with both. No difference.

8. **Draft:** “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.”

   **Source:** “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”

   **Comparison:** Same team, choice, product, prior check and reported capacity. Both demonstratives refer to awaiting-parts and ready-for-work statuses. “After” preserves sequence; the draft does not introduce a claim about the software’s effects on repair performance.

   **Difference test:** Choosing before checking would fail both. The software distinguishing unrelated statuses only would fail both in context. No difference.

### Setup and training

9. **Draft heading:** “Benchline provides setup and training”.

   **Source:** “Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.”

   **Comparison:** The heading describes the documented supplier contribution. “Setup” is given a specific meaning by the following paragraph: configuring the workshop’s choices. It does not assign status definition or responsibility decisions to Benchline. “Training” refers to the recorded online session, not an unspecified ongoing programme.

   **Difference test:** Benchline defining statuses itself would conflict with the following draft sentence and the source, both of which assign that work to the workshop. Unrecorded extra training is not asserted. No finding.

10. **Draft:** “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.”

    **Source:** “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.”

    **Comparison:** Exact wording and allocation of responsibility. The updating decision does not identify the updaters’ names, number or gender. No difference.

11. **Draft:** “Benchline configured those choices”.

    **Source:** “Benchline configured those choices”.

    **Comparison:** Exact wording. The antecedent includes the workshop’s status definitions and its decisions about updating. No difference.

12. **Draft:** “and trained four staff in one online session.”

    **Source:** “and trained four staff in one online session.”

    **Comparison:** Exact number, recipient group, session count and delivery mode. Neither passage gives a session length, staff roles or a total workforce size. No difference.

13. **Draft:** “The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.”

    **Source:** “The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.”

    **Comparison:** Same continuing activity, collection topic and telephone medium. The draft condenses the sentence without asserting any additional communication channel, replaced practice or cessation. The source’s customer relationship is retained by “customer collection arrangements”; the draft leaves the other participants in the calls unstated rather than saying they were different.

    **Difference test:** Calls exclusively about an unrelated topic would fail the draft and source. Calls among staff about customer collections could fit the draft’s less detailed wording, but the draft does not assert that this was the exclusive participant arrangement or contradict the source’s explicit “with customers”. The source supports the stated, more general telephone activity directly. No unsupported fact has been added and no limiting condition on that activity has been removed.

### First interview quotation

14. **Draft:** “In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation”.

    **Source:** “The following is a complete extract from an email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline’s case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale.” Question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?” Vale: “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.”

    **Comparison:** Same person, role, interview medium and date. “Explained the preparation” describes the answer about what the team had to settle; it does not claim a spoken exchange, site visit or observed reaction. The draft does not name the interviewer, but attributes the answer to Vale exactly as the source does.

    **Difference test:** An oral interview, a different interview date or a reporter’s observed scene would differ, but the draft expressly says email and gives the supplied date. No finding.

15. **Draft quotation:** “‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’”

    **Source quotation:** “We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.”

    **Comparison:** The full quotation is exact apart from outer typographic quotation marks. “Had to”, “did not always”, the two locations, and Vale’s wording all remain. The draft attributes the account to Vale; it does not elevate this account into an independently measured result. No difference in meaning, certainty or voice.

    **Difference test:** A part never reaching the correct bench, or its presence always establishing readiness, would change “did not always”; neither change occurs. No finding.

### Trial summary

16. **Draft heading:** “The summary documents visibility”.

    **Source:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Comparison:** “Documents visibility” labels the summary’s recorded statement about staff seeing waiting-for-parts status. The paragraph immediately attributes the statement with “It says”. The heading does not say visibility improved from a measured baseline or imply that the summary measured speed, revenue or satisfaction.

    **Difference test:** A claim of measured improvement would differ from the source, but the heading has no comparative term and its body retains the source attribution. No finding.

17. **Draft:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026”.

    **Source:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026”.

    **Comparison:** Exact document identity, ownership and date. The date modifies the summary, not the start of the trial or the interview. No difference.

18. **Draft:** “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”

    **Source:** “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”

    **Comparison:** Exact count, unit and inclusion condition. The draft does not turn these into 38 completed repairs, 38 customers, all workshop jobs or a comparative assessment of the count. No difference.

19. **Draft:** “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Source:** “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Comparison:** Exact attribution to the summary, staff subject, modal capacity, instrument referent and waiting-for-parts scope. No difference.

20. **Draft:** “The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.”

    **Source:** “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.”

    **Comparison:** Same document and three unmeasured outcomes. The explicit noun replaces a pronoun whose referent is the summary. The draft does not assert that no one measured these elsewhere or that the outcomes did not change.

    **Difference test:** Separate measurement outside the summary would be compatible with both statements. A measured repair-duration result in this summary would fail both. No difference.

### Decision and second interview quotation

21. **Draft heading:** “Vale considers the next step”.

    **Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.”

    **Comparison:** The heading groups the continued-use decision and Vale’s conditional view about future preparation. The body makes the conditional nature explicit with “would”. The heading adds no definite future date, commitment to a new trial or assertion that the review occurred.

    **Difference test:** A promise that the backlog would be added next week would exceed the source but is absent. A conditional consideration of what Vale would do before adding it fits both source and draft. No finding.

22. **Draft:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.”

    **Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

    **Comparison:** Same manager, approval, continued use, new-job scope, backlog postponement and review condition. “Pending” expresses the same unresolved dependency as the source’s “until”. The definite status definitions refer to the workshop’s definitions already described. The draft leaves the review’s actor unstated here; it does not assign the review to someone else.

    **Difference test:** Approval to add the backlog without review would fail both. A completed review is not asserted by either. No finding.

23. **Draft:** “Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote”.

    **Source:** Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” And: “The interview took place by email.”

    **Comparison:** The clause condenses the question’s “again” and “what would you change” into a hypothetical next occasion; it does not assert that another occasion happened or has been booked. “Wrote” preserves the email medium. Attribution remains Vale’s.

    **Difference test:** A definite scheduled second trial would add an event absent from the source, but “would” does not assert one. A spoken answer would conflict with “wrote” and the email source. No finding.

24. **Draft quotation:** “‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’”

    **Source quotation:** “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.”

    **Comparison:** Full quotation exact apart from outer typographic quotation marks. Both occurrences of “would”, “again”, “for new jobs”, “another week”, and the “before adding the backlog” condition remain. It neither says an additional week was actually spent nor turns Vale’s own choice into a recommendation for all workshops. No difference in meaning, certainty or distinctive wording.

    **Source:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Comparison:** “Documents visibility” labels the summary’s recorded statement about staff seeing waiting-for-parts status. The paragraph immediately attributes the statement with “It says”. The heading does not say visibility improved from a measured baseline or imply that the summary measured speed, revenue or satisfaction.

    **Difference test:** A claim of measured improvement would differ from the source, but the heading has no comparative term and its body retains the source attribution. No finding.

17. **Draft:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026”.

    **Source:** “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026”.

    **Comparison:** Exact document identity, ownership and date. The date modifies the summary, not the start of the trial or the interview. No difference.

18. **Draft:** “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”

    **Source:** “records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.”

    **Comparison:** Exact count, unit and inclusion condition. The draft does not turn these into 38 completed repairs, 38 customers, all workshop jobs or a comparative assessment of the count. No difference.

19. **Draft:** “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Source:** “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.”

    **Comparison:** Exact attribution to the summary, staff subject, modal capacity, instrument referent and waiting-for-parts scope. No difference.

20. **Draft:** “The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.”

    **Source:** “It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.”

    **Comparison:** Same document and three unmeasured outcomes. The explicit noun replaces a pronoun whose referent is the summary. The draft does not assert that no one measured these elsewhere or that the outcomes did not change.

    **Difference test:** Separate measurement outside the summary would be compatible with both statements. A measured repair-duration result in this summary would fail both. No difference.

21. **Draft heading:** “Vale considers the next step”.

    **Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.”

    **Difference test:** A promise that the backlog would be added next week would exceed the source but is absent. A conditional consideration of what Vale would do before adding it fits both source and draft. No finding.

22. **Draft:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.”

    **Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

    **Comparison:** Same manager, approval, continued use, new-job scope, backlog postponement and review condition. “Pending” expresses the same unresolved dependency as the source’s “until”. The definite status definitions refer to the workshop’s definitions already described. The draft leaves the review’s actor unstated here; it does not assign the review to someone else.

    **Difference test:** Approval to add the backlog without review would fail both. A completed review is not asserted by either. No finding.

    **Source:** Question: “Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?” Vale: “I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.” And: “The interview took place by email.”

    **Comparison:** The clause condenses the question’s “again” and “what would you change” into a hypothetical next occasion; it does not assert that another occasion happened or has been booked. “Wrote” preserves the email medium. Attribution remains Vale’s.

Third-person singular possessive marking is grammatical; it makes no natural-gender assertion. The source names the workshop, its trial summary and its manager’s backlog decision. The organisational possessives do not invent a human person.
- **“it could distinguish those statuses”:** “It” refers to Benchline, the chosen scheduling product. Third-person singular inanimate reference matches the source’s “it could distinguish these statuses”; no natural gender is conveyed.
- **“who would update them”:** “Who” denotes the person or people selected to update statuses. The construction specifies neither singular versus plural persons nor natural gender. “Them” is plural and refers to the statuses, not to staff. Both features match the identical source sentence.
- **“those statuses”, “those choices”, “the status definitions”:** Plural reference is to the previously described status categories and setup choices. These are things and decisions, with no natural gender. The change from source “these” to draft “those” changes textual distance only.
- **First quotation “We”:** First-person plural; Vale speaks as part of the workshop team, as settled by the source question about “the team” and the preceding account. - **“It says staff could see”:** Third-person singular; “It” is the trial summary, exactly as in the source. “Staff” denotes people collectively without an exact number or natural-gender assertion. The four training recipients are a separate quantified claim; the draft does not equate these groups.
- **“which instruments were waiting”:** Plural relative reference to instruments. No claim about human number or natural gender.
- **Second quotation “I”:** First-person singular, the attributed speaker Vale. The source supplies Vale’s role and name and the identical quotation. First-person singular does not assert natural gender.
- **Second quotation “it again”:** Third-person singular; “it” refers contextually to the scheduling choice and continued use under discussion. The same wording remains in the source quotation. No natural gender.
- **“manager”, “Priya Vale”, “Vale”:** The role and proper name identify the source participant. No “she”, “he” or other natural-gender pronoun has been introduced, and gender is not inferred from the name.

## Quotation and translation findings

Both quotations come from the supplied email interview and reproduce the full attributed answers without repair, welding, new content or removed qualifiers. The draft identifies the interview as email and uses “wrote” for the second answer. No spoken exchange, expression, observed scene or emotional reaction is manufactured. The source states: “Publication of the extract was approved by Vale.” The draft does not invent a separate approval procedure or claim that it performed approval itself.

Source and target are both English. No quotation has been translated. British typographic quotation marks do not change the quoted words. There is consequently no translated-speech obstruction or translation finding.

**Complete.** All factual and attributed passages, headings and implications have been compared, with separate pronoun and quotation checks. **Unresolved findings: none.**

# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

Both quotations come from the supplied email interview and reproduce the full attributed answers without repair, welding, new content or removed qualifiers. # Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source and quotation comparison

Invocation: `/write --genre=casestudy --language=en_GB --output=response source.md`.
Material compared: the complete `source.md` and the complete supplied `draft.md`, including title, standfirst, headings, byline and quotations. Source and target language are English. This review concerns source support and quotation fidelity only.

## Findings

### F1 — The title presents retention as accomplished

**Draft:** “Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs”

**Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source establishes the manager’s approval of continued use. The headline’s ordinary factual reading says Fenwick continues to retain/use the schedule for new jobs. Approval and implementation are different states. The source does not establish implementation after approval.

**Concrete test:** The manager could approve continued use, with that approval awaiting an account renewal or another implementation step; no subsequent new job need have used the schedule. This fits the supplied account and makes the approval true without establishing the headline’s accomplished continuation. Conversely, staff could continue using a schedule without managerial approval; the supplied statement “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” excludes that as an account of this case. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick’s manager approves continued use of its shared schedule for new jobs”. This preserves the headline’s subject matter and warranted certainty, while identifying the established decision.

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

### F2 — The standfirst adds a sequence not established by the material

**Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Also: “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Also: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source states when the trial began, its duration, the summary’s date and the postponement’s condition. It does not say that the manager postponed adding the backlog after the six weeks had elapsed. “After” adds a chronological relationship and implies a completed trial before the postponement.

**Concrete test:** A six-week trial beginning on 20 January could run until 3 March. Its 23 February summary could be an interim summary, and the manager could postpone adding the backlog on 23 February while approving continued use for new jobs. All supplied statements can hold, while “postponed … after a six-week … trial” fails. Neither “trial summary” nor its date explicitly rules out an interim summary. Conversely, postponement after some six-week trial does not establish that this trial began in January or that a team review was its condition; the source expressly supplies those facts. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** Replace the standfirst’s first sentence with: “Fenwick Instrument Repairs’ manager approved continued use of its Benchline schedule for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog pending the team’s review of its status definitions.”

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

The organisation is a normal contextual reference to its manager’s decision. The postponement is supported; “its” associates the backlog with that workshop. |

The added chronology is F2. |
| 4 | “For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.” | Brief: “Write a journalistic customer case in British English for independent repair workshop managers.” / “Show what the customer changed, what the trial established and what its manager would approach differently.” Material: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them.” / “The summary and interview establish the team’s reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.” | This is the writer’s supported framing of the case and its audience. “Shows how” points to the described setup; it does not claim a measured result, causal effect or universal recommendation. | 25 | “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” | “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” | Same decision-maker, action, continuation and job scope. The body preserves approval rather than asserting completed implementation. No finding. |

| “it could distinguish those statuses” | Benchline as the scheduling software; source has “it could distinguish these statuses”. | Third-person singular object of the check. | Inanimate/software reference; no human natural-gender assertion. |

# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source and quotation comparison

Invocation: `/write --genre=casestudy --language=en_GB --output=response source.md`.
Material compared: the complete `source.md` and the complete supplied `draft.md`, including title, standfirst, headings, byline and quotations. Source and target language are English. This review concerns source support and quotation fidelity only.

## Findings

### F1 — The title presents retention as accomplished

**Draft:** “Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs”

**Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source establishes the manager’s approval of continued use. The headline’s ordinary factual reading says Fenwick continues to retain/use the schedule for new jobs. Approval and implementation are different states. The source does not establish implementation after approval.

**Concrete test:** The manager could approve continued use, with that approval awaiting an account renewal or another implementation step; no subsequent new job need have used the schedule. This fits the supplied account and makes the approval true without establishing the headline’s accomplished continuation. Conversely, staff could continue using a schedule without managerial approval; the supplied statement “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” excludes that as an account of this case. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick’s manager approves continued use of its shared schedule for new jobs”. This preserves the headline’s subject matter and warranted certainty, while identifying the established decision.

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

### F2 — The standfirst adds a sequence not established by the material

**Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Also: “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Also: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source states when the trial began, its duration, the summary’s date and the postponement’s condition. It does not say that the manager postponed adding the backlog after the six weeks had elapsed. “After” adds a chronological relationship and implies a completed trial before the postponement.

**Concrete test:** A six-week trial beginning on 20 January could run until 3 March. Its 23 February summary could be an interim summary, and the manager could postpone adding the backlog on 23 February while approving continued use for new jobs. All supplied statements can hold, while “postponed … after a six-week … trial” fails. Neither “trial summary” nor its date explicitly rules out an interim summary. Conversely, postponement after some six-week trial does not establish that this trial began in January or that a team review was its condition; the source expressly supplies those facts. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** Replace the standfirst’s first sentence with: “Fenwick Instrument Repairs’ manager approved continued use of its Benchline schedule for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog pending the team’s review of its status definitions.”

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

# Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’
