# Source and quotation comparison

Invocation: `/write --genre=casestudy --language=en_GB --output=response source.md`.
Material compared: the complete `source.md` and the complete supplied `draft.md`, including title, standfirst, headings, byline and quotations. Source and target language are English. This review concerns source support and quotation fidelity only.

## Findings

### F1 — The title presents retention as accomplished

**Draft:** “Fenwick keeps its shared schedule for new jobs”

**Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source establishes the manager’s approval of continued use. The headline’s ordinary factual reading says Fenwick continues to retain/use the schedule for new jobs. Approval and implementation are different states. The source does not establish implementation after approval.

**Concrete test:** The manager could approve continued use, with that approval awaiting an account renewal or another implementation step; no subsequent new job need have used the schedule. This fits the supplied account and makes the approval true without establishing the headline’s accomplished continuation. Conversely, staff could continue using a schedule without managerial approval; the supplied statement “The manager approved continued use for new jobs” excludes that as an account of this case. No supplied statement excludes the first case.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick’s manager approves continued use of its shared schedule for new jobs”. This preserves the headline’s subject matter and warranted certainty, while identifying the established decision.

Type: source-support finding. No translation is involved.

### F2 — The standfirst adds a sequence not established by the material

**Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog after a six-week Benchline trial.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Also: “The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule.” Also: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The source states when the trial began, its duration, the summary’s date and the postponement’s condition. It does not say that the manager postponed adding the backlog after the six weeks had elapsed. “After” adds a chronological relationship and implies a completed trial before the postponement.

# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source and quotation comparison: draft 2

## Scope and result

Read the complete `source.md` and complete `draft-2.md`, including the title, standfirst, byline, headings and both quotations. The supplied source is the complete package. This comparison covers factual support, attribution, strength, scope, chronology, implications and quotation fidelity. It does not assess general editorial or mechanical choices.

**Result: no source-support findings and no translation findings.** The byline is authorised by the invocation identifying Thomas Barregren; it is not treated as an unsupported attribution because the source brief supplies no author.

The accounting below quotes the source in its original English. References to “the workshop”, “the team” and “the manager” are resolved within the source: Fenwick Instrument Repairs, its workshop team and Priya Vale. The draft does not attribute facts to unnamed outside authorities.

## Complete claim accounting

### Title and standfirst

1. **Draft:** “Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs”.

   **Source:** “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.” And: “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

   **Comparison:** The manager, product and new-job scope are supported. In the context of a case-study headline, “approves” reports the documented approval; it does not supply a new approval date or an approval for every workshop. “Benchline” names the schedule selected and configured in the source. “Continued” is elaborated in the body, which also preserves the backlog exclusion. No change to the subject, certainty or whose decision this was.

   **Difference test:** Approval covering the backlog would differ from the source, but the title restricts the approval to new jobs, and the standfirst expressly states the postponement. A general recommendation for other workshops would differ, but the title names Fenwick’s manager and Fenwick’s use, with no general recommendation. Neither reading establishes a defect in the passage as written.

2. **Draft:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions.”

   **Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.” Also: “The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.”

   **Comparison:** The organisational attribution to Fenwick reports its manager’s workshop decision. “Pending a review” preserves the dependency expressed by “until the team had reviewed”; it does not say the review has happened. “Job status definitions” refers to the statuses for jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work. Neither passage specifies the backlog’s size or the date when it would be added.

   **Difference test:** A completed review or an already-added backlog would fail the source’s postponement and pending condition; the draft asserts neither. An unrelated review would not satisfy “a review of job status definitions”. No supported reading changes the decision or condition.

3. **Draft:** “For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.”

   **Source:** Brief: “Write a journalistic customer case in British English for independent repair workshop managers.” And: “Show what the customer changed, what the trial established and what its manager would approach differently.” Material: “The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session.” And: “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.” And: “The summary and interview establish the team’s reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

   **Comparison:** This is the author’s supported framing of the case for the brief’s audience. It refers to the reported setup process and the summary’s evidential reach. It adds no technical effect or measured outcome. The body supplies both the visibility report and the unmeasured outcomes, preserving the limits.

   **Difference test:** Measured faster repairs or a universal recommendation would exceed the material, but neither is asserted by “how the team set up job statuses” or “what its trial summary could establish”. “Could establish” does not convert the reported experience into a measured improvement. No finding.

### Byline and opening paragraph

4. **Draft:** “By Thomas Barregren”.

   **Support:** The invocation identifies the user as Thomas Barregren, and the brief says: “No author name or call to action is supplied.”

   **Comparison:** Byline treatment is expressly resolved in the assignment. No finding.

5. **Draft:** “In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.”

   **Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” The preceding sentence names Fenwick Instrument Repairs.

   **Comparison:** Same organisation, team, start month, duration, trial and shared bench schedule. The six-week modifier applies to the trial, not to training or rollout. No inference of a particular January start day or February end day.

   **Difference test:** A six-week deployment beginning outside January, or six weeks of training, would differ, but neither meets the draft or source statement. No difference in the claims.

6. **Draft:** “The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments”.

   **Source:** “Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments.”

   **Comparison:** Same workshop and instrument categories. “The workshop” substitutes an established referent. Neither statement excludes additional instrument categories or says that every repair is of one of these types.

   **Difference test:** Brass-only services would fail both statements; additional services would be compatible with both. No difference.

Both quotations come from the supplied email interview and reproduce the full attributed answers without repair, welding, new content or removed qualifiers. The draft identifies the interview as email and uses “wrote” for the second answer. No spoken exchange, expression, observed scene or emotional reaction is manufactured. The source states: “Publication of the extract was approved by Vale.” The draft does not invent a separate approval procedure or claim that it performed approval itself.

Source and target are both English. No quotation has been translated. British typographic quotation marks do not change the quoted words. There is consequently no translated-speech obstruction or translation finding.

**Complete.** All factual and attributed passages, headings and implications have been compared, with separate pronoun and quotation checks. **Unresolved findings: none.**

# Fenwick’s manager approves Benchline for new jobs

Fenwick Instrument Repairs postponed adding its backlog to the Benchline schedule pending a review of job status definitions. For workshop managers, its experience shows how the team set up job statuses and what its trial summary could establish.

By Thomas Barregren

In January 2026, the team at Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. The workshop services brass and woodwind instruments; jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work had previously appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish those statuses.

## Benchline provides setup and training

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to discuss customer collection arrangements by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained the preparation: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary documents visibility

The workshop’s trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction.

## Vale considers the next step

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog pending a review of the status definitions.

Asked what would change next time, Vale wrote: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

SYNTHETIC EVALUATION MATERIAL. Every name, event, quotation and document below is fictional. This is the complete source package. Source language: English.

## Brief

Write a journalistic customer case in British English for independent repair workshop managers. The publisher is scheduling software supplier Benchline; the customer is Fenwick Instrument Repairs. Approximately 250–300 words, in Markdown. Show what the customer changed, what the trial established and what its manager would approach differently. No author name or call to action is supplied.

## Material

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule. Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets. The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses.

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers.

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. Question: “What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?”
